title: Milestone: Classical Music
objective: After this level you can connect the eras of classical music from Bach to the Romantics.
summary: In 1829 the 20-year-old Mendelssohn revived Bach's St. Matthew Passion. The Romantic century ran from Beethoven's Heiligenstadt Testament to The Nutcracker.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. The century that looked forward also looked back.
cards.body: This chapter ran from Beethoven's Vienna to Tchaikovsky's St. Petersburg: feelings first, stars on stage, nations in sound. But one of the era's biggest moments was a performance of music by a composer who'd been dead for decades.

cards.headline: Bach, brought back by a 20-year-old
cards.body: On 11 March 1829, at the Singakademie in Berlin, Felix Mendelssohn, aged 20, conducted Johann Sebastian Bach's St. Matthew Passion: its first performance since Bach's death in 1750. Britannica says the concert launched the 19th-century Bach revival. So the Romantics didn't only chase the new. They also taught audiences to hear the past again.

cards.headline: Milestone: the Romantic century
learned: Why Romantic composers put feeling first, using music to tell stories and speak for one person.
How Beethoven stretched Classical forms, and how he kept composing after losing his hearing.
Why virtuosos like Paganini and Liszt drew crowds like stars, while Chopin preferred small rooms.
How composers used folk tunes, dances and legends to give their nations a sound of their own.

questions.prompt: From Level 42: how did Beethoven hold conversations from 1818 on?

options.label: Through sign language he invented
options.rationale: He used notebooks.

options.label: With a hearing aid that restored his hearing
options.rationale: Ear trumpets helped little; he turned to writing.

options.label: Visitors wrote in notebooks and he answered aloud
He stopped speaking to anyone
options.rationale: More than 130 conversation books survive.

questions.explanation: In his conversation books, visitors wrote their side and Beethoven usually answered out loud.

questions.prompt: From Level 44: the word 'rubato' comes from the Italian for what?

options.label: To sing
options.rationale: It's about time being 'stolen' and given back.

options.label: To dance
options.rationale: It's about flexible time, not dance.

options.label: To whisper
options.rationale: Rubato is about timing, not volume.

questions.explanation: Rubato, from rubare, 'to rob': some beats are stretched and others hurried.

questions.prompt: From Level 45: who coined the word 'Lisztomania' in 1844?

options.label: Frédéric Chopin
options.rationale: Chopin was Liszt's friend, not the word's coiner.

options.label: Niccolò Paganini
options.rationale: Paganini inspired Liszt but didn't name the craze.

options.label: Richard Wagner
options.rationale: Not him.

questions.explanation: Heinrich Heine named the frenzy around Liszt's concerts 'Lisztomania' in 1844.

questions.prompt: From Level 46: what made Verdi's Falstaff, premiered when he was 79, a rematch?

options.label: It was his first opera after a long illness
options.rationale: The rematch was with comedy.

options.label: His only other comedy had flopped half a century earlier
It was Wagner's opera, rewritten by Verdi
options.rationale: Falstaff is Verdi's own, after Shakespeare.

options.label: It reused the music of Nabucco
options.rationale: It was new music for a comedy.

questions.explanation: Falstaff (1893) was his second comedy; the first, at the same theater, had failed about fifty years before.

questions.prompt: Beethoven's Fifth opens short-short-short-long. Which ingredient from Levels 1 and 4 is that pattern?

options.label: Harmony
options.rationale: Harmony is notes at once; this is about timing.

options.label: Pitch
options.rationale: The pattern is about lengths, not how high the notes are.

options.label: Tempo
options.rationale: Tempo is the speed of the beat, not the pattern of long and short.

questions.explanation: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds over the beat; the Fifth's motif is a rhythm first.
